title: Convert all employee names to uppercase.
shortTitle: Convert all employee names to uppercase

s1_definition.profdef: This is a `map` transformation that applies `String.toUpperCase()` to each name, producing a new stream of upper-cased strings. It is a value-level transform, one input to one output, and the original strings are untouched because strings are immutable in Java.
s1_definition.analogy: The HR clerk at the National Bank of India is preparing name badges, and the printer requires all names in capital letters. She retypes each name in capitals on the badge. `map` with toUpperCase is exactly that — taking each name and producing its capitalised version.
s1_definition.oneliner: `map(String::toUpperCase)` turns every name into its capitalised form, leaving the originals unchanged.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This is a `map` transformation that applies `String.toUpperCase()` to each name, producing a new stream of upper-cased strings. It is a value-level transform, one input to one output, and the original strings are untouched because strings are immutable in Java.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The HR clerk at the National Bank of India is preparing name badges, and the printer requires all names in capital letters. She retypes each name in capitals on the badge. `map` with toUpperCase is exactly that — taking each name and producing its capitalised version.

**One line to remember:** `map(String::toUpperCase)` turns every name into its capitalised form, leaving the originals unchanged.

sections.s2_technical:
The `map` method applies a function to each element. Here the function is the string method `toUpperCase`, so `stream.map(String::toUpperCase)` converts every lowercase or mixed-case name into all capitals. The method reference `String::toUpperCase` is an instance-method reference on the element itself, which the compiler understands as calling toUpperCase on each incoming string.

Strings in Java are immutable, so toUpperCase does not change the original string — it returns a brand new string. This means the source list of employees is unaffected; map produces a separate stream of new capitalised strings that you collect into a new list. Immutability is why this transformation is completely safe even if the original data is shared.

A subtle but important detail is locale. The no-argument toUpperCase uses the default locale of the machine, which can produce surprising results for certain languages — the classic example is the Turkish dotless letter i. In a bank that runs across regions, the safe habit is to specify a locale explicitly, for example `name.toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT)` or `Locale.ENGLISH`, so the output is deterministic regardless of the server's locale.

A senior nuance: if names can be null you must guard before calling the method, either by filtering nulls out first or by mapping through a null-safe helper, because calling toUpperCase on null throws a null pointer exception.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India prints physical access badges for staff, and the badge printer firmware requires every name in uppercase for legibility on the security scanner. The HR system stores names in normal mixed case like Rajesh and Priya. Before sending the batch to the printer, every name must be converted to capitals, but the master record must stay in its original casing. This is exactly how a map with toUpperCase works — each name is transformed to capitals into a new list while the originals remain untouched.

The code defines an `Employee` with a name. A `BadgeService` exposes `upperCaseNames(List<Employee>)` using map with a locale-safe uppercase transform. The runnable `Main` feeds mixed-case names and logs the capitalised badge names.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three names — Rajesh, priya (lowercase), Amit.

Step 1: The stream opens over three employees.

Step 2: The first map pulls out each name, so the stream now carries the strings Rajesh, priya, Amit.

Step 3: The second map applies toUpperCase with Locale.ROOT. Rajesh becomes RAJESH, a new string; the original Rajesh object is untouched because strings are immutable.

Step 4: priya, which was lowercase, becomes PRIYA, proving the conversion works regardless of starting case.

Step 5: Amit becomes AMIT.

Step 6: `collect` gathers the three capitalised strings into a new list, while the employee master retains its original mixed-case names.

```
Oct 30, 2026 11:30:05 AM com.bank.badge.service.BadgeService upperCaseNames
INFO: Converting 3 names to uppercase for badges
Oct 30, 2026 11:30:05 AM com.bank.badge.Main lambda$main$0
INFO: Badge names: [RAJESH, PRIYA, AMIT]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: Stream<Employee> [Rajesh, priya, Amit]
    │
    ▼
  map(Employee::getName)  → Stream<String> ["Rajesh","priya","Amit"]
    │
    ▼
  map(s -> s.toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT))   (returns NEW strings; originals immutable)
    ├─ "Rajesh" → "RAJESH"
    ├─ "priya"  → "PRIYA"
    └─ "Amit"   → "AMIT"
    │
    ▼
  collect(toList())  →  ["RAJESH","PRIYA","AMIT"]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
To convert values I use the map operation, applying the string method toUpperCase to each name, which produces a new stream of capitalised strings. Because strings in Java are immutable, toUpperCase never changes the original — it returns a brand new string — so the source list of employees is completely safe and I simply collect the transformed values into a new list.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India this was for printing physical access badges. The badge printer firmware required names in uppercase for the security scanner, but our HR master stores them in normal mixed case like Rajesh and Priya. So before sending the batch to the printer I streamed the employees, extracted each name, and mapped it to its uppercase form, leaving the master record in its original casing.

A senior point I always raise is locale. The no-argument toUpperCase uses the machine's default locale, which can give surprising results for some languages — the famous example is the Turkish dotless letter i, which does not uppercase the way English expects. Because the bank runs across regions, I specify the locale explicitly, using Locale.ROOT or English, so the output is deterministic no matter which server runs the job. I also guard against null names before calling the method, because calling toUpperCase on a null reference would throw a null pointer exception.
